# Bandhanamokkhajātaka (Ja 120)

**ID:** Ja 120
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Bandhanamokkhajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bandhanamokkhajātaka* (Ja 120) is the tenth and concluding discourse of the *Hamsivagga* in the *Ekanipāta* of the Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1877]. Its opening canonical verse begins with the line *Abaddhā tattha bajjhanti* ("Whilst folly’s speech") [Fausböll 1877]. According to the narrative framework of the commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana to address false accusations leveled against him by the brahmin ascetic Ciñcā (Ciñcamāṇavikā), remarking that she had made similar slanderous accusations against him in past lives [Fausböll 1877]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta was the royal chaplain (*purohita*), the king was a past birth of Ānanda, and the treacherous queen was Ciñcamāṇavikā; after extricating himself from danger, the chaplain renounces worldly wealth, undertakes the ascetic life in the Himalayas (*Himavanta*), and attains the higher knowledges and absorptions to reach the Brahmaloka [Fausböll 1877].

Scholars of folklore and comparative literature observe that along with the *Mahāpadumajātaka* (Ja 472), the *Bandhanamokkhajātaka* preserves one of the oldest Indian attestations of the widespread narrative motif of "Potiphar's wife" (the spurned woman's false accusation) [Aris and Aung San Suu Kyi 1979]. In Burmese art and epigraphy, the jātaka is depicted on glazed terracotta plaques and murals in numerous eleventh- to thirteenth-century temples at Pagan (Bagan)—including the Ananda, Thingaraza, and Wetkyi-in Gubyaukgyi—where it is inscribed under the title *Bandhanamokkha* or spelling variants such as *Bandhanamukkha*, *Bandhanāmukha*, and *Hatthawutha* [WinThanTun 2002].
